questions.stem: Business change is best described as:
options: the replacement of a business's chief executive officer
a business moving its head office to a new address
any alteration to the way a business operates
an increase in net profit from one year to the next
questions.explanation: Business change is any alteration in how a business operates, including its processes, structure, technology, products or culture. A new chief executive or a move are examples of particular changes, not the concept itself.

questions.stem: A proactive approach to change involves:
options: changing only when new legislation leaves the business no choice
anticipating forces for change and acting before problems arise
responding to change only once it has been forced on the business
avoiding change so that the business remains stable and predictable
questions.explanation: A proactive manager looks ahead, anticipates pressures and opportunities, and changes before being forced to. Responding only once change is forced on the business is the reactive approach.

questions.stem: After a competitor opens nearby and its sales fall by 20 per cent, a Bendigo hardware store cuts prices and extends its trading hours. This is an example of:
options: a proactive approach to change
organisational inertia
a restraining force for change
a reactive approach to change
questions.explanation: The store changed only after the competitor arrived and sales had already fallen, so it was reacting to pressure. A proactive approach would have anticipated the threat and acted beforehand.

questions.stem: Why might managers prefer a proactive approach to change over a reactive one?
options: it ensures that employees will never resist any of the changes that are introduced
it allows change to be planned carefully and can give an advantage over competitors
it guarantees that the business will never face any pressure from external forces
it means that no money needs to be spent until problems have actually appeared
questions.explanation: Acting early gives managers time to plan, consult and implement change in an orderly way, and may let the business move ahead of rivals. No approach can guarantee an absence of external pressure or employee resistance.

questions.stem: A small Ballarat retailer waits until customers start complaining before it updates its outdated website. A likely reason managers take this reactive approach is that:
options: reacting late always costs less than planning change in advance
a reactive approach gives the business an edge over its competitors
legislation prevents small businesses from changing before problems arise
they have limited time and money to research and plan for future trends
questions.explanation: Small businesses often lack the time, money or expertise to scan the environment and plan ahead, so they respond only when a problem appears. Reacting late can be costly and usually leaves the business behind competitors rather than ahead.

questions.stem: The percentage of market share is:
options: a business's net profit as a percentage of its total revenue
the percentage of the business's shares owned by its founders
the percentage of the business's customers who make a complaint
a business's sales as a percentage of total sales in its market
questions.explanation: Market share compares a business's sales with total sales in its market, showing how it performs against competitors. Net profit as a percentage of revenue is a measure of profitability, not market share.

questions.stem: A Perth sports retailer has annual sales of $3 million in a local market with total sales of $24 million. What is its market share?
options: 8 per cent
1.25 per cent
87.5 per cent
12.5 per cent
questions.explanation: Market share = 3 ÷ 24 × 100 = 12.5 per cent. Dividing the other way, 24 ÷ 3, gives 8, which is not a percentage of the market.

questions.stem: Riverside Plumbing Supplies had revenue of $900,000, cost of goods sold of $400,000 and other expenses of $350,000. What was its net profit?
questions.explanation: Gross profit is $900,000 − $400,000 = $500,000, and net profit is $500,000 − $350,000 = $150,000. Stopping at $500,000 gives gross profit, which ignores the other expenses.

questions.stem: The level of staff turnover measures:
options: the quantity of output produced per employee per hour
the number of injuries suffered by staff during the year
the rate at which employees leave and have to be replaced
the percentage of working days lost through staff absence
questions.explanation: Staff turnover shows how often employees leave and must be replaced, which can signal dissatisfaction and adds recruitment and training costs. Days lost through absence is the rate of absenteeism.

questions.stem: A Canberra call centre employed an average of 80 staff over a year. During the year, 20 staff left and were replaced. What was its rate of staff turnover?
options: 75 per cent
25 per cent
20 per cent
4 per cent
questions.explanation: Staff turnover = staff who left ÷ average number of staff × 100 = 20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25 per cent. Taking the 20 leavers as the percentage ignores the size of the workforce.

questions.stem: A business has 200 employees who each work 250 days a year. In the year, 1500 days were lost to unplanned absence. What was its rate of absenteeism?
options: 0.3 per cent
3 per cent
7.5 per cent
6 per cent
questions.explanation: Total working days = 200 × 250 = 50,000, and 1500 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 3 per cent. The figure 7.5 is the average number of days lost per employee, not a percentage.

questions.stem: A rise in a business's rate of staff absenteeism is most likely to indicate:
options: a fall in the number of complaints from customers
low employee motivation or job satisfaction
a rise in the business's share of its market
an improvement in the productivity of its workforce
questions.explanation: When employees are unhappy, stressed or unmotivated, they are more likely to take unplanned days off, so rising absenteeism is a warning sign for human resource management. It also tends to lower productivity rather than raise it.

questions.stem: A bakery made 1000 loaves using 50 labour hours last year. This year it made 1100 loaves using the same 50 labour hours. What was its rate of productivity growth?
options: 9.1 per cent
10 per cent
2 per cent
22 per cent
questions.explanation: Productivity rose from 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 to 1100 ÷ 50 = 22 loaves per hour, and (22 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 10 per cent. Dividing the increase by the new figure, 2 ÷ 22, gives 9.1 per cent, which uses the wrong base.

questions.stem: A rising level of wastage on a production line suggests:
options: an inefficient use of inputs that raises costs
an improvement in the efficiency of operations
a rise in the business's share of its market
an improvement in staff morale and motivation
questions.explanation: More wastage means more materials are used for each unit of good output, which is inefficient and adds to costs. It points to problems in operations such as poor processes, equipment or training.

questions.stem: Which key performance indicator most directly measures customer satisfaction with a service?
options: the rate of staff absenteeism
the level of wastage
the number of workplace accidents
the number of customer complaints
questions.explanation: Customer complaints reflect customers' experience of the business, so a rise suggests falling satisfaction. Absenteeism, wastage and accidents measure internal matters such as staff and operations.

questions.stem: An online retailer's number of website hits doubled over a year, but its number of sales stayed the same. Which is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: the retailer's share of the online market has doubled over the year
the retailer's net profit has doubled along with its website traffic
the retailer's staff productivity has fallen by half over the year
more people are visiting the site, but the extra visits are not becoming sales
questions.explanation: Website hits measure visits, not purchases, so unchanged sales show that the extra visitors are not buying. Market share and net profit depend on sales, which did not change.

questions.stem: A rise in the number of workplace accidents at a Pilbara mine site is most likely to point to:
options: better working conditions on site
higher customer satisfaction
lower levels of staff turnover
poor safety training or procedures
questions.explanation: More accidents suggest weaknesses in safety training, equipment or procedures, which also raise costs and harm morale. It indicates worse, not better, working conditions.

questions.stem: Over two years, Riverbend Motors' net profit rose by 15 per cent, while its market share fell from 18 per cent to 15 per cent. Which is the best interpretation?
options: the business is growing faster than all of its competitors in the market
the total size of the market must have shrunk over the two years
net profit and market share must always rise and fall together
profit has grown, but the business is losing ground to its competitors
questions.explanation: A falling market share means competitors' sales are growing faster than Riverbend's, even though its profit has risen. The data cannot show whether the total market shrank, and profit and market share can move in different directions.

questions.stem: Lewin's Force Field Analysis is used to identify and assess:
options: the driving and restraining forces acting on a proposed change
the four drives that motivate employees in the workplace
the steps of unfreezing, changing and refreezing a business
the generic strategies that a business can use to compete
questions.explanation: Force Field Analysis lists the forces pushing for a change and those resisting it, so managers can judge whether and how to proceed. Unfreezing, changing and refreezing are the steps of Lewin's separate Three-step Change Model.

questions.stem: In Force Field Analysis, weighting means:
options: placing the forces in order from strongest to weakest
putting the planned change into action in the business
checking whether the change has met its objectives
giving each force a score that shows its strength
questions.explanation: Weighting assigns each driving and restraining force a value, for example from 1 to 5, to show how strong it is. Placing the forces in order by those scores is ranking, the next step.

questions.stem: After weighting each force, a manager lists the forces in order from strongest to weakest to decide which to deal with first. This step of Force Field Analysis is:
options: ranking
weighting
evaluating the response
implementing a response
questions.explanation: Ranking orders the forces by their weightings so managers can prioritise the most significant ones. Weighting is the earlier step of giving each force a score.

questions.stem: A manager weights the forces for a new system. Driving: competitors 4, cost reduction 5, technology 3. Restraining: employees 4, financial considerations 3, time 2. According to Force Field Analysis:
options: the restraining forces total 12 and outweigh the driving forces of 9, so the change should not proceed
the forces are equal in total weighting, so the business remains in a state of equilibrium
the change cannot proceed while any restraining force has a weighting greater than 2
the driving forces total 12 and outweigh the restraining forces of 9, so the change can proceed
questions.explanation: The driving forces total 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 and the restraining forces 4 + 3 + 2 = 9, so the forces for change are stronger. Lewin held that change occurs when driving forces outweigh restraining forces, not when every restraining force has gone.

questions.stem: When the driving forces for a change outweigh the restraining forces, implementing a response involves:
options: abandoning the change because some restraining forces remain
ignoring the restraining forces because they have been outweighed
adding new restraining forces to slow down the pace of change
strengthening driving forces and weakening restraining forces
questions.explanation: Managers implement the change while acting on the forces, such as building support for the drivers and reducing resistance. Ignoring restraining forces is a common mistake, because they can still cause the change to fail.

questions.stem: In Force Field Analysis, evaluating the response involves:
options: placing each of the forces in order from the strongest to the weakest
listing all of the forces for and against the change before it starts
reviewing data such as KPIs to see whether the change achieved its aims
giving each driving and restraining force a score to show its strength
questions.explanation: After the change, managers check its results, for example by comparing key performance indicators with targets, to judge whether it worked. Scoring and ordering the forces are weighting and ranking, which come before the change.

questions.stem: Which is a driving force for change in business?
options: globalisation
organisational inertia
time
financial considerations
questions.explanation: Globalisation pushes businesses to change, for example to compete with overseas firms or reach new markets. Organisational inertia, time and financial considerations are restraining forces in the study design.

questions.stem: New Victorian laws require food outlets to stop using certain single-use plastic packaging. For a takeaway chain, this legislation acts as:
options: a restraining force for change
an example of organisational inertia
a key performance indicator
a driving force for change
questions.explanation: The law requires the chain to change its packaging, so it pushes the business towards change. Legislation can be a restraining force when it prevents or slows a change, but here it is forcing one.

questions.stem: Growing customer demand for ethically sourced clothing leads a Melbourne fashion label to change its suppliers. Which driving force is this?
options: organisational inertia
societal attitudes
legislation
technology
questions.explanation: Changing community values and expectations, such as concern for ethical sourcing, are societal attitudes. No law is requiring the change, so legislation is not the force at work.

questions.stem: The owners of a Toowoomba printing firm push to switch to digital printing because it will cut production costs by a third. Which driving force is most evident?
options: time
societal attitudes
reduction of costs
organisational inertia
questions.explanation: The main reason for the change is to lower production costs, which is the driving force of reduction of costs, here pushed by the owners. Organisational inertia and time are restraining forces.

questions.stem: Which force for change can act as either a driving force or a restraining force?
options: globalisation
legislation
pursuit of profit
organisational inertia
questions.explanation: Legislation can force a business to change, such as new safety laws, or stop a change, such as planning rules blocking an expansion, so it appears on both lists. Organisational inertia only resists change, while profit and globalisation push for it.

questions.stem: A rival café chain opens three stores in the same Geelong suburb, and the owner of an established café decides she must modernise her menu and service. Which driving force is most evident?
options: time
financial considerations
competitors
legislation
questions.explanation: The pressure to change comes from the actions of rival businesses, which is the driving force of competitors. Time and financial considerations are restraining forces.

questions.stem: Organisational inertia is best described as:
options: the pressure created when new competitors enter a business's market
the rate at which employees leave a business and need to be replaced
a law that slows the speed at which a business is allowed to change
the tendency of a business to resist change and keep its existing ways
questions.explanation: Organisational inertia is resistance to change built into a business's routines, structures and culture, so it keeps doing things the way it always has. It comes from within the business, not from competitors or the law.

questions.stem: Staff at a Newcastle bank fear they will lose their jobs because of new software and refuse to use it. Which restraining force is this?
options: legislation
time
financial considerations
employees
questions.explanation: Employees resisting change because of fear of job loss, the unknown or retraining are a restraining force. Nothing in the case concerns laws, deadlines or the cost of the change.

questions.stem: A small Barossa winery wants to install robotic bottling equipment but cannot afford its $2 million cost. Which restraining force is preventing the change?
options: financial considerations
organisational inertia
legislation
managers
questions.explanation: The cost of the change is more than the business can afford, so financial considerations are holding it back. Organisational inertia would be a reluctance to change ways of working, not a lack of funds.

questions.stem: Middle managers at a Sydney insurer oppose a plan for a flatter structure because they would lose authority and status. This shows:
options: managers acting as a driving force
legislation acting as a restraining force
employees acting as a driving force
managers acting as a restraining force
questions.explanation: Managers can drive change, but here they resist it because it threatens their position, so they are a restraining force. Managers appear in the study design as both a driving and a restraining force, depending on whether they support the change.

questions.stem: A business must introduce a new booking system before the busy Christmas period but has only six weeks to retrain all of its staff. Which restraining force is most evident?
options: time
legislation
organisational inertia
societal attitudes
questions.explanation: The short period available to implement and train for the change is the restraining force of time. Nothing suggests the business is reluctant to change, so organisational inertia is not the main force.

questions.stem: Porter's lower cost strategy involves:
options: offering products customers see as unique so a premium price can be charged
relying on government subsidies so that prices can be cut below cost
offering the widest range of luxury products available in the market
becoming the lowest-cost producer in the industry
questions.explanation: A lower cost strategy aims to produce at lower cost than all competitors, allowing the business to charge lower prices or earn higher margins. Offering unique products at a premium is the differentiation strategy.

questions.stem: Porter's differentiation strategy involves:
options: becoming the lowest-cost producer so prices can be set below competitors
copying competitors' products exactly and selling them at the same price
reducing product quality so that costs fall below the industry average
offering products customers see as unique, so a premium price can be charged
questions.explanation: Differentiation makes a product stand out through features such as quality, design, branding or service, so customers will pay more for it. Producing at the lowest cost is the lower cost strategy.

questions.stem: A Daylesford chocolate maker uses rare single-origin cacao, hand-finished designs and luxury packaging, and charges well above its rivals. Which strategy is it following?
options: lower cost
a reactive approach to change
organisational inertia
differentiation
questions.explanation: The business makes its product distinctive and charges a premium price for it, which is differentiation. A lower cost strategy would focus on keeping costs and prices below rivals.

questions.stem: A discount furniture chain uses flat-pack designs, bulk buying and self-service warehouses to keep its costs below those of every rival. Which strategy is it following?
options: a proactive approach to change
organisational inertia
lower cost
differentiation
questions.explanation: Keeping costs below all competitors through efficient methods and scale is Porter's lower cost strategy. Differentiation would rely on making the product unique rather than cheap to produce.

questions.stem: Which is a risk for a business that follows a lower cost strategy?
options: costs rise because it must use luxury inputs and specialised staff
a rival may find cheaper methods and remove the cost advantage
customers may be unwilling to pay the premium price for its products
the business cannot sell high volumes because its prices are high
questions.explanation: A cost advantage lasts only while the business remains the lowest-cost producer, so a rival with better technology or scale can erode it. Customers refusing to pay a premium is a risk of differentiation, not of a lower cost strategy.
